FirstIntroduction: ^Hey there—! 'm Suzy. I'm in charge of everything you see on screen. Sprites, colors, movement, pixel collisions... I'm your one chip animation studio!
^I operate at 16 MHz - four times faster than Mikey. Not that I'm bragging...Okay, maybe a little~
^But enough about me! What brings you to this old motherboard?
^> Honestly, this whole thing fascinates me.
^> I just wanted to see how games worked back then.

c-0: ^Love that. Not many people take the time to notice what goes on inside their machines!
c-1: ^Retro detective, huh? You’re in the right place.
c-2: ^Weird is underrated. You’ve got a good brain. I like you already ;)!
^You ask the right kind of questions. Curious, grounded... you’d make a decent engineer. Or artist. Or both! Want to know how I work? I promise it’s cooler than it sounds.

ReturningIntroduction: ^> Could you explain your role here again?
^> Mind if I have another go at 'Collision Control'?

c-1: ^Love your enthusiasm! Need a quick refresher?

Questions: ^> Do you have any unique tricks for processing graphics?
^> Any chance I could see you in action?

c-0: ^Okay, picture this: You want a spaceship zooming across the screen. You don't just throw me an image and say "go". I need two things:
^2. A Sprite Control Block: basically a set of instructions telling me how to handle it.
^Give me those, and I'll blit that thing onto the screen buffer in no time.
c-1: ^Ah, my secret sauce! I have a technique that no other consoles at my time have figured out.
^While I'm drawing, I also keep an eye out for overlaps. Each sprite gets a collision number - sort of like a name tag, numbered 0 to 15.

^If two sprites overlap, I record the highest number into something called the collision depository. You (or your game code) can check it afterward to see what hit what. And yes - this is pixel-perfect. None of that rectangle-guessing nonsense other consoles are used to.
c-2: ^Absolutely! I'm actually really well known for reusing graphics to be more efficient, I'm super proud of it.

^One piece of pixel data, let's say a robot, can be reused in multiple SCBs. I can draw it in different spots, scales, or colours without duplicating the actual image data. Saves memory and still looks great, Win win!
c-3: ^I can do you one better! I'll let you try your hand at 'Collision Control'!

CollisionControlInstructions: ^Just press the SPACE BAR whenever you see two objects collide on-screen.
^Sounds simple but its quite tough! You sure you're ready?

c-0: ^I love your confidence, Let's get started!
c-1: ^In the meantime, make sure you meet Mikey if you haven't already.

b: ^That task can get really hectic at times but you held your own pretty well.
^Here, take this 'Collision Control' badge as a token of my appreciation!
^Tough isn't it? Would you like to try again?

c-1: ^Feel free to come back and try again whenever you'd like.

FirstIntroduction: ^Hi there. (He adjusts his glasses, looking up from his clipboard.)
^You don't look like you're from around here. Curious visitor, huh?
^I'm Mikey, the main processor of the Lynx. That said, I wouldn't get very far without Suzy. She's faster, louder... and never lets me forget it.
^But I manage the system’s brain: logic, inputs, audio, and timing. I keep things running smoothly at 4 MHz, methodical, one cycle at a time.
^Say, how’s your day going so far?
^> Honestly? Kinda great. I’ve never seen anything like this.
^> It’s cool, kinda surreal. Everything’s so... alive in here.
^> I’m just happy to learn something new.

c-0: ^That’s good to hear. Always nice when someone shows up with an open mind.
c-1: ^I’m glad you feel that way. There’s a lot going on under the surface—literally.
c-2: ^That’s an excellent mindset. Curiosity is how you make the invisible visible.
^Honestly? My days are always productive. Busy, but satisfying. That’s the joy of structure, you always know what comes next.
^Anyway, if you’re interested, I’ve got time for some questions. Or I can show you what I’ve been working on.

ReturningIntroduction: ^Oh, you're back. Wanna give me a hand?
^> Could I ask you a question?
^> Yeah, what do you need me to do?

c-1: ^We're doing 'Byte Runner', do you still remember it?

Questions: ^> How does an 8-bit CPU like you work?
^> What kind of sound can you make?
^> Anything I can help you with?

c-0: ^I'm based on the 6502 family of processors. Classic architecture. I handle 8 bits of data at a time; meaning I process numbers from 0 to 255 in a single operation.
^Larger numbers? More complex math? I break them down and handle them step by step. It's slower, sure, but it works. No floating point, no shortcuts. Just pure byte-by-byte logic.
^I operate within a 16bit address space, which gives me 64 kilobytes of memory. That's the total memory I can access at once; for code, variables, assets, everything.

^It sounds small by today's standards, but with proper structure and clever loading, it's enough. And we were the pioneers of our time. Suzy, for instance, knows how to reuse graphics. I myself also admire that efficiency.
c-1: ^I control a 4 channel sound system. Each channel plays its own waveform: like square waves, sawtooth, or noise.

^You set the pitch, volume, and length, and I handle the playback. I can even mix in digital samples, though that's more demanding. I'm no synthesizer, but I do a good job delivering clean, retro audio.
c-2: ^I work closely with Suzy, handling video timing - starting the screen refresh cycle, managing blanking intervals, and making sure Suzy doesn't draw in the middle of a frame.
^If you've ever seen screen tearing in a game, that's what happens when graphics and timing go out of sync. I make sure that never happens here.
^Although I handle a lot of tasks, handling anything more than one task at a time isn't my thing especially not how modern systems do. Don't get me wrong though I do move fast, so it feels smooth.
^I run a main loop, one task at a time: check input, update logic, refresh screen, repeat.
c-3: ^Sure, it would be nice to have another helping hand around here. Would you like to try and allocate some bytes for me, experience for yourself how an 8-bit processor works? Join me in 'Byte Runner'!

ByteRunnerInstructions: ^Don't worry it's simple, I'll send you address signals down the bus - you read 'em, and drag my byte workers into the right memory slots before Suzy hogs the line again!

c-1: ^No stress, come back whenever you're ready.

Introduction: ^This is the Lynx's screen. What you’re looking at is a TFT LCD with double buffering.
^Double buffering means Suzy can draw the next frame in memory while the current one is still being shown—so the screen never flickers.
^It’s a technique still used in graphics today.

c-0: ^That’s right! When graphics and screen refreshes aren’t in sync, you get tearing. Double buffering avoids that.
c-1: ^Not quite. Memory leaks are a different kind of problem.
c-2: ^Nah, that’s a power issue, not a graphics one. But fair guess.

Introduction: ^This is the Lynx's main RAM, which contains 64 kilobytes of fast access memory.
^64k...that sounds like a lot, right? But wait, modern computers have 32,000,000 KB!
^Everything: game code, graphics, sound...must fit into this space at runtime.
^It’s not much, but used cleverly, it’s enough to run entire worlds.
^Want to test your memory on memory?
Quiz: ^How much RAM does the Lynx have?

c-0: ^You got it! That’s 65,536 bytes: tight quarters, but doable.
c-1: ^Too generous. This isn’t a modern system.

Introduction: ^Tiny but mighty. The Lynx speaker can play four separate sound channels at once.
^Each channel plays a waveform: square, sawtooth, or even noise. Mikey mixes them in real time.
^Care to put your ears to the test?
Quiz: ^How many audio channels can the Lynx play at once?

c-0: ^Yep! Four channels, handled entirely in hardware.

Introduction: ^This switch routes power to the LCD backlight circuit: the light behind the screen that lets you play in the dark.
^On old handhelds, the backlight is one of the hungriest parts. Flip this on, and a DC/DC regulator boosts and smooths the voltage so the lamp gets clean power without flicker.
^Meanwhile, the main board still has to power Mikey and Suzy at stable logic levels so the Lynx uses regulation and capacitors to keep the rails steady when the backlight kicks in.
Quiz: ^Why does turning on the LCD backlight drain the battery faster on retro handhelds?
^> The backlight draws significant current, so the regulator has to supply more power.
^> The CPU underclocks itself and wastes energy as heat.
^> The screen turns black, so the pixels consume extra power.

c-0: ^Exactly. The backlight is a big load; more current out means the batteries empty sooner. Good regulation keeps the rest of the system stable.
c-1: ^Not quite. Underclocking usually *reduces* draw; the real hog here is the lamp’s current.
c-2: ^Nope. The backlight behind the LCD is the main power consumer, not the dark pixels.
